summary: The Little Red Lighthouse under the George Washington Bridge: an 1880 Sandy Hook tower moved here in 1921, dark from 1947, owned by New York City Parks since 1951.

structures.note: Built at Sandy Hook, N.J., as the North Hook Beacon; reconstructed at Jeffrey's Hook in 1921 (designation report; 40 ft)

staffing.status: part-time keeper (1921); Coast Guard responsibility for aids from 1939

access.note: Grounds in Fort Washington Park. The USLHS guide says the interior is open on select summer days; the Historic House Trust says visitors to the annual festival can climb to the lantern room.

visit.note: Interior open on select days in summer and at the annual festival (see access note)

facts.agency: New York City Department of Parks & Recreation

events.note: Cast-iron tower erected at Sandy Hook, N.J., as the North Hook Beacon (not this site)
Wood post light with two oil lanterns, fixed red; established 1 November 1889
Light-House Board asks for a larger light and a fog bell
Sandy Hook tower dismantled; the beacon replaced with a skeleton tower
Tower moved from Sandy Hook and reconstructed at Jeffrey's Hook
10 October 1921: 100 cp acetylene red lamp, flashing every 3 s (LPC); the 1921 Bulletin says 'fixed red to flashing white'
Machine-operated fog bell, one stroke every 15 seconds, two weeks after the light
Ground broken for the George Washington Bridge; light to be moved during construction
Aeronautical beacon placed on the George Washington Bridge
Last year the light was in use with signals unchanged (designation report)
Coast Guard decommissioned the lighthouse; lamp extinguished
Coast Guard property transferred to the Department of Parks of the City of New York, 23 July 1951
Listed as Jeffrey's Hook Lighthouse, part of a Hudson River lighthouses thematic nomination (NRHP 79003130)
Restoration by NYC Parks, 1982 to 1986 (designation report); 1986 renovation of $209,000
New York City landmark, LP-1654, designation list of 14 May 1991
Historic House Trust announces an initial $13 million restoration (release dated 29 September 2026)

corrections.why: 12.2 m is the tower's height (40 ft, designation report). The designation report gives the 1921 focal plane as 61 ft (18.6 m) above water. The current focal height is not verified.

corrections.current: The US Lighthouse Society's archive lists it as not open to the public.

corrections.why: The access note predates the 2026 announcement and the Society's own guide says the interior opens on select days.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1880 date and the Sandy Hook origin belong to the cast-iron tower, which was moved and reconstructed here in 1921 (designation report). The USLHS record's 'Year Tower Established: 1918' is not matched by any source read; the story follows the designation report and the 1921 Bulletin.
Last in use through 1947 (designation report); the Coast Guard decommissioned the lighthouse in 1948 (USLHS guide). The record's 1947 is the last year in use.
The fog bell was placed in commission in October 1921, two weeks after the light was changed (designation report).

notes_for_editor: Disagreements stated in the story: (1) the 1921 colour and characteristic: the designation report says a flashing red light (and summarises the light as flashing red); the 1921 Bulletin (PDF p. 43, printed p. 203, page image checked) says 'fixed red to flashing white'; the USLHS guide says the light flashed white. The current characteristic in the record (Fl R 3s) is not checked against a current Light List. (2) The late-1920s part-time keeper: the USLHS roster names William Knapp (at least 1926); the designation report names Bill Collins (note 16, citing a newspaper research file). The story says the sources do not reconcile them. (3) Laborers Roache and Whitely (1909, 1911) predate the 1921 tower; the roster gives only the heading Laborer. (4) Access disagreement: USLHS place record 'Open to Public: No'; USLHS guide 'open to the public on select days during the summer'; the 2026 Historic House Trust release says festival visitors can climb to the lantern room. (5) Checked against page images: Bulletin 1921 PDF p. 15 ('Jeffrys Hook', printed p. 175), PDF p. 43 (illuminant and fog-signal entries, printed p. 203), Bulletin 1927 PDF p. 44 (date and quoted sentence, from text). Page images of the Bulletins are OCR-interleaved; the printed wording was read off the image. (6) The 1895 item 323 (scan p. 249) gives the '$3,000 ... for say' estimate, cited to the 1895 report in the story; the 1900 item 406 (scan p. 78) gives the 'permission' wording; the 1899 report (item 399) repeats the permission wording. (7) The Historic House Trust release is dated 29 September 2026 on its page and refers to the festival on Saturday 3 October; the story gives the release date. The Trust's release and the Society's teaching guide are quoted only in short phrases or paraphrase (the guide reproduces LighthouseFriends material, all rights reserved). (8) The NRHP nomination for 79003130 is not digitised (npgallery placeholder); the 1979 listing rests on the designation report and the USLHS guide (which gives 29 May 1979, not used). NYC Parks highlights page refused (HTTP 403). Wikipedia and Wikidata are not cited in the story. (9) No wreck or rescue at the light was found in the sources read, so the chapter is omitted. other_stations for keepers not researched (person pages not fetched).
